items.text:
「Claude Fable 5.2が出たから全部切り替えよう」と思った人は（Claude Codeの人も、APIの人も）、切り替える前にこれだけ

Claude公式が11/9に出した「どのモデルを使うか」ガイドの結論は、意外にも「ほとんどの作業はOpus 5.5の標準（effort medium）から」です

公式ガイドで分かること
・Claude Codeの標準モデルはOpus 5.5。API料金はFable 5.2の半分（Fable 5.2は入力$8・出力$40／100万トークン）
・Fable 5.2に上げるのは、大きな移行や設計、長時間まかせる作業、Opus 5.5をhighにしても足りないとき
・足りないと感じたら、モデルより先に effort（考える量）を1段上げる。それでも足りなければ上のモデルを低めのeffortで試す
・今のClaude Codeでは、ファイル探しのExploreサブエージェントも会話と同じモデルで動く。Fableにすると調べ物までFableになる

明日から何をするか
・Claude Codeで /effort status を打って、今のeffortを確認する
・Fableは重い作業1つだけ /model で切り替えて試し、/usage で使った量を見比べる（切り替える前に /compact）

YOUR CODING AGENT RE-LEARNS YOUR REPO EVERY SESSION. YOU PAY FOR IT.
@MSFTResearch's free plugin, TokenEconomizer, cut 18–31% off Claude Code and Codex costs in their tests.

What it trims:
→ Tools you never call (they stop riding along with every request)
→ Stuck loops: it nudges the agent, never kills the run
→ Repo quirks, like the test command that works (off by default, extra calls)

Free, Apache-2.0, no signup or key. Claude Code, Codex 0.141+, Copilot CLI; Cursor is experimental.

The math: a $200/month agent bill drops about $37–62 if your repo behaves like their SWE-Bench runs.

Builder tip: install it in the repo you open daily, since it learns from past sessions there. Tool pruning edits your agent's settings; `toolprune restore` undoes it.

Verdict: worth a clone if you live in one repo. Numbers are the authors' own, and Pass@1 dipped 1 point with Opus 4.8 on Claude Code.

I've FINALLY wrapped my FREE, open-source course on building a coding agent from scratch!

• 8 in-depth articles.
• 6 video lessons.
• 1 complete roadmap to mastering harness engineering.

Over the past few months, I've studied the internals of Claude Code, OpenCode, Pi, and Aider to understand what makes coding agents work.

And I noticed the agent loop is the easiest part.

The actual engineering happens in the harness.

Things like:

• Context management
• Sandboxing
• Permissions
• Memory
• Tool execution
• Evaluations

So I've turned everything we learned into a practical course where you build a fully functional Claude Code clone.

Here's the complete 8-step roadmap:

1. Harness Architecture: Design the core agent system and its components.
2. Agent Loop: Build the reasoning and tool execution loop from scratch.
3. Sandboxing: Execute code safely using Docker and Modal.
4. Context Engineering: Implement memory, skills, compaction, and LSP.
5. Subagents: Run parallel agents with isolated context windows.
6. Remote Execution: Deploy agents to the cloud using CLI, webhooks, and cron jobs.
7. Evaluations: Build benchmarks and regression tests with Opik.
8. Recording & Replay: Reproduce failures and verify fixes with Kitaru.

By the end, you'll have a working coding agent with an interactive terminal interface AND a headless runtime for running agents remotely.

You can even try the finished agent before starting the lessons.

Everything is written in Python.
And the entire codebase is open source under Apache-2.0.

A HUGE thank you to @modal, @Cometml, and @zenml_io for sponsoring this course and helping us keep it 100% FREE.

Whether you're an AI engineer or a software engineer transitioning into AI, this is the roadmap I wish I'd had when learning harness engineering.

Get the complete course on GitHub: https://t.co/JmCajfijIP

And follow along with the articles on Substack: https://t.co/MLZHZRdRmd

P.S. If you find it useful, give the repo a star so more engineers can discover it.

You get a remote MCP server working in one coding agent. Then you open the next agent, paste the same server in, and it never connects. Same URL, same token, but every tool wants it written its own way.

@brandononchain mapped out how one hosted MCP server runs in Claude Code, Cursor and Codex. An MCP server is an endpoint that hands your agent extra tools, and a hosted one lives at a single URL all three can point at.

In Codex, it goes in a server table in the TOML config, with the URL plus the name of the environment variable that holds your token. Adding a hosted MCP URL straight from the Codex command line is in the official docs now too.

Claude Code wants a JSON entry, and a hand-written one has to say it's an HTTP server or Claude Code quietly skips it. Cursor reads its own JSON file and writes environment variables in a slightly different style.

Each tool also has its own way to show whether the server connected, so check there before blaming the server. One server, three config dialects, and the fix is usually the one field that differs.
